records.statement: In a speech of 12 November 2015 to the Trades Union Congress, Andrew G Haldane, Chief Economist of the Bank of England, discussed smart machines and artificial intelligence as substitutes for human work, asked what these labour-market trends imply “for the economy and monetary policy”, and set out how a flat rather than rising labour share would lower the MPC’s projected paths for wages and inflation.
records.qualification: AI is one part of a wider technological change (“smart machines”, the “Second Machine Age”), as in Carney 2018; the monetary-policy passage concerns the substitution of capital for labour in general and a projection scenario, not AI alone or a policy decision. The speaker’s view, with disclaimer.

evidence.passage: One source of such advantage is that Artificial Intelligence (AI) – the machine brain - differs in several important respects from human intelligence – the human brain.
Turning to the nearer-term, what if any implications do these labour market trends carry for the economy and monetary policy?
That might arise because technology has made it easier and cheaper than ever before to substitute labour for capital, man for machine. That is the very essence of the Second Machine Age hypothesis.
So how different might the MPC’s projections look if the labour share was, say, flat rather than rising over the next few years?

crossFamily.result: drafted under decisions 5a and 11a; earliest-located role moved here from Carney 2018 (correction). Second check (2026-11-04): earliest located text and qualified whole-text articulation agreed (blind search A1.2 found the same speech; a scenario, not a causal finding).
crossFamily.headline: Correction under decision 5a: the headline moves from Carney (14 September 2018) to this speech (12 November 2015), located by the checker (A1.6) and read here on 2026-11-04. Both are speeches.

records.statement: De Nederlandsche Bank’s discussion paper of 25 July 2019 on general principles for the use of AI in the financial sector, which presents DNB’s preliminary view, states that many of the prerequisites for a responsible application of AI are already covered by existing regulations, in particular the requirements on sound and controlled business operations.

time.note: Publication day from DNB’s release “DNB komt met richtlijnen voor gebruik kunstmatige intelligentie”, read here on 2026-11-04 (source dnb-2019-release: “Gepubliceerd: 25 juli 2019”, the paper “vandaag … gepubliceerde”), as the cross-family checker reported (second check, B24 and C29). The PDF prints ©2019.

records.qualification: A discussion paper of preliminary views inviting comment, not final policy. The same passage states that loopholes in regulation may exist, that societal expectations may go beyond current rules, and that legislators and supervisors are considering AI-specific policies or regulations; it does not state that no separate framework is needed. The paper names an author, Joost van der Burgt (PDF p. 2), and presents DNB’s view; the English wording is not authenticated against a July 2019 capture.

evidence.passage: De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) presents its preliminary view on a set of possible principles in this discussion paper.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 33, chapter 4 ‘General principles for the use of AI by financial institutions (‘SAFEST’)’
evidence.passage: On the one hand, this implies that many of the prerequisites for a responsible application of AI are already covered by existing regulations. In particular the requirements regarding sound and controlled business operations (see Financial Supervision Act articles 3:10, 3:17 and 3:18 for legal context) cover many aspects.
Moreover, loopholes in regulation may exist and societal expectations may go beyond what current regulations require.

crossFamily.result: drafted under decision 11a; read here on 2026-11-04 from a copy obtained through the session's web-fetch tool (curl refused). Second check (2026-11-04): institutional comparator and preliminary-view articulation agreed; publication day 25 July 2019 from DNB’s release, read by the checker and here; loopholes and possible AI-specific policy kept.
crossFamily.headline: The earliest located institutional text for U12 moves from DP5/22 (11 October 2022) to this paper (25 July 2019), as the checker found (A1.12). Brainard (13 November 2018) stays the earliest located text.

records.statement: The joint consultation paper of BaFin and the Deutsche Bundesbank of 15 July 2021 on machine learning in risk models states that, since the current regulatory foundations are worded in a technology-neutral manner, they are largely transferable to the characteristics of machine-learning methods, with only a few places where adaptation might be necessary.
records.qualification: A consultation paper on risk models of banks and insurers (Pillars 1 and 2), inviting comment; it states the authorities’ view at that date, not final policy, and names a few places where adaptation might be necessary.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 4, chapter I ‘Machine learning is advancing’
evidence.passage: since the current regulatory foundations are worded in a technology-neutral manner, they are largely transferable to the characteristics of ML methods, with only a few places where it might be necessary to adapt the regulatory foundations.

The following joint consultation paper of BaFin and Deutsche Bundesbank deals with the concrete use of machine learning (ML) in risk models of Pillars I and II of the regulatory frameworks for banks and insurers.

crossFamily.result: new record from the follow-up pass (decision 11a, open leads). Second check (2026-11-04): articulation agreed (broad transferability of technology-neutral foundations, few possible adaptations).

records.statement: The joint consultation paper of BaFin and the Deutsche Bundesbank of 15 July 2021 states that the use of machine-learning methods can help to quantify risks more accurately and enhance process quality, thereby improving financial firms’ risk management.
records.qualification: A statement of possibility in the paper’s introduction; the paper does not report measured improvements.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 3, chapter I ‘Machine learning is advancing’
evidence.passage: The use of ML methods can help to quantify risks more accurately and enhance process quality, thereby improving financial firms’ risk management.

The following joint consultation paper of BaFin and Deutsche Bundesbank deals with the concrete use of machine learning (ML) in risk models of Pillars I and II of the regulatory frameworks for banks and insurers.

crossFamily.result: new record from the follow-up pass (decision 11a, open leads). Second check (2026-11-04): articulation agreed; a consultation, no measured performance claim.

records.statement: The joint consultation paper of BaFin and the Deutsche Bundesbank of 15 July 2021 states that, as machine-learning models become more complex, their calculations become less transparent for modellers, users, validators and supervisors, making the modelling harder to comprehend and the validity of model output harder to check.
records.qualification: The paper also states that the black-box characteristic can be justified by higher predictive ability and that explainable-AI methods are promising; it concerns risk models under Pillars 1 and 2.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 13, chapter III.3 ‘Focus on explainability’
evidence.passage: the details of the calculations are less transparent for modellers, users, validators and supervisors. As a result, it is more difficult to comprehend the modelling and, if applicable, to check the validity of the model output as well.

The following joint consultation paper of BaFin and Deutsche Bundesbank deals with the concrete use of machine learning (ML) in risk models of Pillars I and II of the regulatory frameworks for banks and insurers.

crossFamily.result: new record from the follow-up pass (decision 11a, open leads). Second check (2026-11-04): articulation agreed, with the model-performance trade-offs kept.

records.statement: In a speech published on 21 May 2026, Ida Wolden Bache, Governor of Norges Bank, said that Norges Bank is exploring how AI and machine learning can be applied in its modelling system, that preliminary results are promising, and that machine learning can help improve forecasting models.
records.qualification: The speaker’s account of work in progress at Norges Bank; preliminary results, not an adopted model. No disclaimer is printed on the page.

evidence.passage: We are currently exploring how artificial intelligence and machine learning can be applied in the modelling system. Preliminary results are promising.
For example, machine learning can help improve forecasting models and lead to more flexible methods for weighting models to reduce forecasting error.

crossFamily.result: new record from the follow-up pass (decision 11a, open leads). Second check (2026-11-04): articulation agreed; preliminary work, no adopted model.

records.statement: In a speech of 29 January 2026, Ole Christian Bech-Moen, Executive Director of Monetary Policy at Norges Bank, said that Norges Bank is assessing how AI will affect the neutral rate and therefore its assessment of interest-rate levels, and that to the extent AI boosts productivity AI could contribute to an increase in the neutral rate.
records.qualification: The Norwegian speaking notes (“Talepunkter til presentasjonen”, published with the Norwegian page on 29 January 2026 at 16:00) are the original published expression; the English text, on the English page published on 2 February 2026, is a machine translation post-edited by Norges Bank, as it states, so its wording is not the delivered wording. Both are published notes, not a transcript of the delivered speech. The speech illustrates possibilities with model simulations and states no policy decision. No disclaimer is printed.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 8, slide ‘“Real-time” estimates and model estimates of the neutral real rate’
evidence.passage: And so here we are today, in real time, wondering how AI will affect the neutral rate and therefore our assessment of interest rate levels in the slightly longer term.
To the extent that AI boosts productivity ahead or economic agents believe strongly enough that this will happen, AI could contribute to an increase in the neutral rate.
This translation was generated by ChatGPT and post-edited by Norges Bank.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 8, plansje on the neutral real rate (Norwegian speaking notes)
evidence.passage: I den grad KI løfter produktiviteten fremover – eller at aktørene i økonomien tror sterkt nok på at det vil skje – kan KI bidra til en oppgang i den nøytrale renten.
evidence.note: The original Norwegian of the second English quotation.

crossFamily.result: new record from the follow-up pass (decision 11a, open leads). Second check (2026-11-04): articulation and delivery date agreed; the Norwegian speaking notes, located by the checker, are recorded as the original published expression and the English text as Norges Bank’s post-edited machine translation.

records.statement: Danmarks Nationalbank’s Analysis of 21 January 2019 on text-based machine learning and bankruptcy modelling states, in its summary, that machine-learning methods make data modelling more flexible and allow unstructured data to be used, and that using them to include auditors’ remarks and management reports substantially increases the accuracy of calculated bankruptcy probabilities.
records.qualification: Quoted from the Danish summary on the landing page; the PDF of the Analysis (No. 3, read 2026-11-04, the same bytes as the cross-family checker’s copy) states the same finding in its summary (“Det øger nøjagtigheden af de beregnede konkurssandsynligheder”). The PDF credits Anna Kirstine Hvid and Pia Mølgaard, Quantitative Risk Analysts, Financial Stability (p. 7), and prints no statement that the views are theirs alone: the voice is the Nationalbank’s analytical series, with staff credits, not a claim that the text is anonymous. The modelling serves the Nationalbank’s financial-stability analysis; the underlying working paper of November 2018 is a separate document, not recorded.

evidence.passage: Benyttes sådanne metoder til at inddrage revisorpåtegninger og ledelsesberetninger fra virksomheders regnskaber til at beregne deres konkurssandsynlighed, øges nøjagtigheden af beregningen væsentligt.
evidence.note: Translation: if such methods are used to include auditors’ remarks and management reports from firms’ accounts in calculating their bankruptcy probability, the accuracy of the calculation increases substantially.

crossFamily.result: new record from the follow-up pass (decision 11a, open leads). Second check (2026-11-04): articulation agreed; the PDF, now read, credits two staff analysts and prints no views disclaimer, so the voice stays institution, qualified.

records.statement: ECB Working Paper No. 352 of April 2004, by Paul McNelis and Peter McAdam, reports that “thick” models combining several neural-network models outperform the best-performing linear models in real-time and bootstrap inflation forecasts for euro-area service-price indices, and do as well or sometimes better for consumer and producer price indices across several countries.
records.qualification: A staff working paper under the ECB disclaimer; one co-author is outside the ECB. It uses neural networks, a machine-learning technique, without the words “machine learning” or “artificial intelligence”, and reports results for particular indices and periods, not general superiority (the non-technical summary says linear and neural-network forecasts converge in periods without structural change).

evidence.passage: Thick models represent “trimmed mean” forecasts from several neural network models. They outperform the best performing linear models for “real-time” and “bootstrap” forecasts for service indices for the euro area, and do well, sometimes better, for the more general consumer and producer price indices across a variety of countries.
We show in this paper that the linear and neural network specifications converge in their forecasts in such periods.

crossFamily.result: new record from the pass before 2016; takes the earliest-located role (correction). Second check (2026-11-04): earliest located text and articulation agreed (blind search A1.1 found the same paper; gains specific to index, country and period).
crossFamily.headline: Correction: the headline moves from the Bank of England staff working paper of September 2017 to this ECB staff working paper (April 2004), found in the pass before 2016. It also precedes the Czech National Bank paper of 2005 (a lead, decision 16a). Agreed by the second check’s blind search (A1.1). The checker also read the Bank of Canada working paper of January 1999 (a lead, decision 16a) and the Bank of England’s One Bank Research Agenda of February 2015 (C32), which is later than this paper.

records.statement: BCBS Working Paper No. 4 of December 2000, by Ranjana Sahajwala and Paul Van den Bergh, describes the “supervisory risk assessment and early warning systems” of G10 supervisors that use “artificial intelligence” in software to replicate examiners’ financial analysis, and states that an effort is under way to combine the potential of artificial intelligence of software with expert human judgement to produce accurate risk assessments of banks.
records.qualification: A staff working paper under the series disclaimer, surveying supervisors’ practice. “Artificial intelligence” here denotes expert systems and ratio-based software that replicate an examiner’s analysis, not machine learning; the paper also describes statistical models of bank condition. It describes use and effort under way, not a recommendation by the Committee.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 19, section on financial ratio and peer group analysis
evidence.passage: These frameworks are also termed “general expert systems” for their use as distinct, stand-alone risk assessment systems.

In addition, an increased effort is under way to combine the potential of artificial intelligence of software with expert human judgement in order to produce accurate risk assessments of banking institutions.
Supervisory authorities currently using the risk assessment and early warning systems covered by this paper find them useful in their ongoing risk-focused banking supervision process.

leads.item: BaFin, “Big data meets artificial intelligence – challenges and implications for the supervision and regulation of financial services”, report of 16 July 2018 put to public consultation (https://www.bafin.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/dl_bdai_studie_en.pdf; read 2026-11-04 by text search only). It discusses black-box models (PDF pp. 14, 37) and says that supervisory and regulatory bodies “must be technology-neutral” (p. 4). Cited by the 2021 BaFin–Bundesbank paper.
leads.reason: BaFin alone is not among the bodies the scope names; the scope's opening names “banking and market supervisors” in general. Whether a national supervisor that is not a central bank enters is a scope question (open question in the review note). It would not be earlier than U04’s holder (June 2017); on U12 it would precede Brainard (November 2018) only if a passage states broad coverage, which the text search did not find. Maintainer decision of 2026-11-04 (open question 1 of the follow-up pass): as recommended, the BDAI report stays a lead, on the logic of decision 16a.
